componentIdea.title: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

guidingQuestion: How do food and fuel provide energy?
If energy is conserved, why do people say it is produced or used?
chapterOverview.purpose: This component idea helps students make sense of how stored energy—often originating from the Sun—is captured, transformed, and used in everyday life, while recognizing that not all energy remains useful after it is transferred.
chapterOverview.centralIdeas: Energy in the environment exists in forms that are not immediately useful for everyday needs. “Producing energy” refers to capturing stored energy (frequently traced to the Sun) and converting it to a useful, transportable form (e.g., batteries, food, fuel). Energy is not destroyed when “used”; it typically spreads to the environment in less useful forms (often as heat). Designing systems for efficiency maximizes useful output and minimizes waste, cost, and unintended impacts.

table.access: Rubbing hands or objects together creates warmth.

table.focus: Energy is converted, not created, and can be captured, stored, and released.
table.access: Energy from the Sun, food, fuel, and batteries.

table.focus: Chemical reactions store and release energy in arrangements of C, H, and O; heat is a common byproduct.
table.access: Combustion, respiration, photosynthesis (arrangements of major atoms).

table.focus: Multistage chemical/physical processes capture and release energy with desirable and undesirable byproducts.
table.access: Cellular mechanisms; solar and alternative energy capture and transport.

progression.narrative: Understanding begins with tangible warming from friction and the Sun, then expands to everyday stores and conversions of energy (food, fuel, batteries). In middle school, students connect energy changes to chemical reactions (photosynthesis captures energy; respiration and combustion release it) and to efficiency and waste heat. In high school, students apply conservation principles across complex systems, quantify transfers, and reason about efficiency, environmental impacts, and sustainability.

standards.statement: Make observations and conduct experiments to provide evidence that friction produces heat and reduces or increases the motion of an object.
standards.bigIdea: When surfaces rub, motion changes and noticeable warmth can be produced.
scientificIdeas: When two surfaces rub, they can slow down and become warm—this effect is friction.
Friction can slow or stop sliding or rolling objects.
Friction warms the surfaces that rub against each other.
Greater changes in motion typically produce more warming.
Rougher surfaces generally create more friction and warming.
Pressing surfaces together harder increases friction.
Lubricants (e.g., soap, oil) reduce friction and warming.
Some machines rely on friction (e.g., brakes); others reduce it (e.g., wheels, axles).
studentIdeas: Friction only slows things down; it doesn’t create warmth.
Rubbing or moving creates energy from nothing.
All friction is bad and should always be avoided.
All surfaces make the same amount of friction regardless of texture or pressure.

standards.statement: Develop a model to explain how food is utilized through chemical reactions to form new molecules that support growth, resulting in the release of energy as matter moves through an organism.
standards.bigIdea: Food is made of carbon-based molecules that store energy captured from the Sun; rearrangements of atoms in reactions (e.g., digestion/cellular respiration) release that energy to support life functions.
scientificIdeas: "Food" is plant matter or tissues of organisms that consume plants.
Food consists primarily of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen arranged by plants using energy from the Sun.
Different atomic arrangements store different amounts of energy; rearrangements can capture or release energy.
Breaking down and rearranging food molecules releases energy used by the organism.
Living systems can only release usable energy from a subset of carbon-based molecules.
The energy in food ultimately came from sunlight captured via photosynthesis.
Some plant/animal tissues are not consumed; over geologic time, their stored energy can transform into fossil fuels.
studentIdeas: Food is only for growth; it doesn’t release energy.
All chemicals are usable energy sources; some are avoided only because they’re poisonous.
Energy from food is added without a chemical process.
All substances we consume (e.g., water, vitamins) provide energy.
